intro: Copenhagen's oldest surviving trees trace back to specific, named people rather than to a park or forest: a sailor who may have brought home a mulberry to feed Christian IV's silkworms, the botanist Frederik Liebmann who carried a cycad back from Mexico in 1842, and the sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen, whose black locust supposedly grew from Italian seed. The fourth entry belongs to no one in particular: a lime avenue in the king's own garden that has simply outlasted every replanting around it since the 1660s.
meta_description: Copenhagen's most remarkable trees: Christian IV's silk mulberry, Thorvaldsen's black locust, a 1842 Mexican cycad, and a student tradition's linden.
question_answer: Copenhagen's oldest tree is generally considered the mulberry at Proviantgarden on Slotsholmen, dating to King Christian IV's early 17th-century attempt to build a Danish silk industry by planting mulberries to feed silkworms. It is likely 350 to 420 years old.
question_meta: The Proviantgarden mulberry, planted for Christian IV's 17th-century silk venture, is Copenhagen's oldest tree at roughly 350 to 420 years old.
question_context: King Christian IV pursued a Danish silk industry the way several of his European contemporaries were doing in the early 1600s, by planting mulberry trees to feed silkworms rather than importing raw silk. Almost nothing survives of that venture beyond a street name, Silkegade, and this one tree, standing at Proviantgarden on Slotsholmen, part of the naval arsenal Christian IV built from 1603 to supply his warships. Tradition credits its planting to a sailor who brought the tree home from Asia rather than a court gardener, and it has stood long enough to have watched tall ships come and go from the harbor basin the arsenal once fronted, well before Slotsholmen became the seat of Denmark's parliament and courts. The island's naval buildings have since changed jobs entirely, now government offices rather than stores for rope and ships' biscuit, but the mulberry keeps leafing out every spring regardless. No precise planting date survives, only its association with Christian IV's long reign, which is why this project gives it a wide, honest age range rather than a single invented number.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Copenhagen?
faq.a: The mulberry at Proviantgarden on Slotsholmen, planted during Christian IV's early 17th-century silk industry attempt and likely 350 to 420 years old.

faq.q: Is the Palm House cycad really that old?
faq.a: Yes. Botanist Frederik Liebmann brought it from Mexico in 1842, and it remains the Botanical Garden's oldest living specimen, roughly 184 years old.

faq.q: Did Thorvaldsen really bring his own tree home from Italy?
faq.a: Tradition says so: the black locust beside Thorvaldsens Museum is said to have grown from seed the sculptor carried back when he returned to Copenhagen in 1838, though this is tradition rather than documented fact.

Along Husalle in Kongens Have, the king's garden beside Rosenborg Castle. Garden historians describe them as among the oldest living trees in Denmark, unlike the castle's two more formal linden avenues, which have been replanted repeatedly since the 1660s and 1700s.

trees.name: The Mulberry of Proviantgarden
trees.story: King Christian IV tried to build a Danish silk industry the way his contemporaries elsewhere in Europe were doing it, by planting mulberry trees to feed silkworms, and this is the one tree from that entire royal venture that anyone can still point to. It stands today at Proviantgarden, part of the naval arsenal Christian IV built on Slotsholmen from 1603 to supply his warships, on ground that once fronted a working harbor basin where vessels docked to be provisioned and armed. Tradition credits a sailor who brought it home from Asia rather than a court gardener, and it has stood long enough to have watched those same tall ships come and go for provisions centuries before Slotsholmen became the seat of Denmark's parliament and courts. The Danish silk venture itself mostly failed; Copenhagen's climate never suited silkworms the way Christian IV hoped, and the street name Silkegade nearby is now the closest most Copenhageners get to the story. This tree is the exception, a specimen one detailed historical account describes as having remarkable vitality, still leafing out every spring in a courtyard surrounded by 17th-century naval buildings that have long since changed jobs, now government offices rather than stores for rope and ships' biscuit.
trees.access: Free, open access, public courtyard on Slotsholmen
trees.transport: Christianshavn metro station or Copenhagen Central Station, short walk across Slotsholmen
trees.notes: The Christian IV silk-industry origin and the tree's location and vitality are described consistently across Trae.dk's detailed feature on Copenhagen's valuable trees and a local heritage site's history of Proviantgarden, though both ultimately appear to draw on the same underlying historical account rather than fully independent research. No source names the exact species; White Mulberry (Morus alba) is given here because it is the species historically used for silkworm cultivation, which the sources' own silk-industry framing implies, but this is inference rather than a directly sourced identification. No precise planting date exists, only the association with Christian IV's reign (1588-1648), hence the wide age range.

best_time.label: June into July, when the mulberries ripen and drop

trees.name: The Ancient Cycad of the Palm House
trees.story: In 1842, the Danish botanist Frederik Liebmann sailed to Mexico and came home with, among other specimens, a small cycad that looked more like a stunted pineapple than anything resembling a tree. It has spent nearly two centuries since then growing at its own unhurried pace in Copenhagen's Botanical Garden, first at the garden's earlier city-centre site and then, from 1874, in the Palm House built specifically to keep tropical and subtropical plants alive through Danish winters. Cycads are not actually related to palms or ferns despite resembling both; they are among the oldest living groups of seed plants on Earth, largely unchanged since long before flowering plants existed, which makes a 184-year-old specimen barely middle-aged by the standards of its own family. Liebmann died in 1856 at just 43, only 14 years after bringing the plant home, but his cycad has outlived him by more than a century and a half and remains, by the garden's own account, its oldest living specimen and one of its genuine star attractions, a slow-growing plant that has simply outlasted everyone who ever went looking for one.
trees.access: Paid entry to Palmehuset (the outdoor Botanical Garden itself is free)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk
trees.notes: The Liebmann collection date (1842), his death (1856), and the plant's status as the garden's oldest living specimen are given by the Danish Wikipedia entry on the Botanical Garden; only one detailed source found for this specific specimen, flagged accordingly, though the garden's own move to the current Palm House in 1874 is independently well documented. Coordinates are the garden's street address, not a surveyed position within the Palm House.

trees.name: Thorvaldsen's Robinia
trees.story: Bertel Thorvaldsen spent more than 40 years in Rome becoming Europe's most celebrated Neoclassical sculptor before returning home to Copenhagen in 1838 to a hero's welcome, and this multi-stemmed black locust growing beside the museum built to house his life's work is said to have come home with him, grown from seed he carried back from Italy. Denmark's dendrological society surveyed the tree in 1995 and recorded a trunk over three metres around, splitting into several stems rather than one, and estimated its age at up to 155 years at that time, consistent with a planting soon after Thorvaldsen's actual return. That would put the tree, and not just the museum, among the direct physical legacies of a sculptor whose bronze and marble work now sits in collections from the Vatican to Warsaw. Black locust is not a species anyone would plant deliberately for its connection to fine art. It is a hardy, fast-growing tree valued more for binding loose soil and producing useful timber than for looking distinguished, which makes its adoption into Thorvaldsen's own story feel almost like an accident that stuck, a workmanlike species growing beside one of Europe's grandest personal museums, surveyed precisely enough by Danish tree recorders in 2008 to give this project one of its few confirmed coordinates.
trees.access: Free, open access, public ground beside Thorvaldsens Museum
trees.transport: Christianshavn metro station or Copenhagen Central Station, short walk across Slotsholmen
trees.notes: The only detailed source found is the Danish Dendrological Society's own tree register entry, which itself frames Thorvaldsen's personal planting as tradition ('possibly brought Robinia seeds') rather than documented fact; flagged accordingly. Measurements (3.2m circumference, 1995) and coordinates (surveyed 2008) come directly from that official register, making the location one of this city's most precisely confirmed.

best_time.label: May, when it flowers in heavy white clusters

trees.name: The Husalle Lindens
trees.story: Kongens Have is Copenhagen's oldest public park, laid out from 1606 for King Christian IV beside his new Rosenborg Castle, and its formal linden avenues were planted soon after: Kavalergangen and Damegangen, the two clipped alleys nearest the castle, date to around 1664 and 1700. Almost none of those original trees survive; both avenues have been replanted more than once in the four centuries since. Husalle, a third avenue running parallel to the garden's main axis a little further north, has fared differently: its lindens are described by garden historians as among the oldest living trees in Denmark, having escaped the repeated replacements that emptied the more formal avenues nearer the castle of their original planting. The garden itself has survived far more than ordinary wear. It has hosted royal pleasure grounds, public promenades, and, in recent years, a summer sound installation that lets speakers hidden in ten of its trees tell stories to anyone who walks close enough to trigger them, a very modern use for trees old enough to have shaded Danish kings centuries before recorded sound existed. Husalle's lindens do their storytelling the old way, simply by having outlasted almost everything planted around them.
trees.access: Free, open access, Kongens Have (public park, open daily)
trees.transport: Norreport railway and metro station, short walk
trees.notes: Kongens Have's founding (1606) and the c.1664/c.1700 planting of Kavalergangen and Damegangen are documented by the official Danish heritage agency's Trap Danmark entry and corroborated by Danish Wikipedia; both also state that virtually no original trees remain in those two avenues. The claim that Husalle's lindens are 'among the oldest in the country' comes from the same sources but without an exact planting date for that specific avenue, so the age range given here (300-360 years) reflects the garden's documented 1660s-1700s planting era generally rather than a dated record for Husalle itself. This entry represents the avenue as a whole rather than a single named tree.

trees.name: The Temple Tree of Landbohøjskolens Have

location.address: Landbohøjskolens Have (Fakultetets Fredede Have), entrance at Bülowsvej / Thorvaldsensvej, Frederiksberg

trees.story:
This ginkgo is male, and the female it pollinates lives on the other side of the street. The two trees have never touched. The university library, writing up the garden's own history, calls it the largest ginkgo in the collection and gives 1883 as its planting year, which would make it about 143. That date comes from that one source and nowhere else, so read it as the garden's account rather than a measured fact.

It is planted in the middle of a large stone mound, which is a strange thing to do to a tree and suits this one. Ginkgo biloba is the last surviving member of a lineage older than flowering plants, and the Danish name for it, tempeltræet, points at the temple courtyards in China and Japan where the final populations were kept alive by monks while the wild ones disappeared. The garden around it was laid out in 1858 for the Royal Veterinary and Agricultural College and has been legally protected since 1965.

Protection is not immortality. The blood beech planted the year the garden opened, which the official heritage listing still describes as the thickest tree here, was felled in 2018. Nothing suggests the ginkgo has gone the same way and the species is famously hard to kill, but the newest dated confirmation we could find of this one is not recent. The garden is free and open from sunrise to sunset.

best_time.label: late October into November, when it turns gold and drops the whole crown within a week

trees.access: Free, open to the public sunrise to sunset (university garden, protected since 1965)
trees.transport: Frederiksberg metro station, roughly 5-8 minute walk

trees.name: The Handkerchief Tree of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section A, near the northeast corner (Nørrebrogade / Kapelvej), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
What looks like flowers on this tree are leaves. For roughly two weeks in May the handkerchief tree hangs hundreds of paired white bracts through its crown, each pair a modified leaf wrapped around a small dark ball of actual flower, and Danish names it better than English does: duetræ, the dove tree. Davidia involucrata grows wild in the mountains of western China and reached Western cultivation only in 1904, through the plant hunter Ernest Wilson. It is still an uncommon thing to find in Denmark, and this one is multi-stemmed, so in May the bracts come at you from several directions at once.

Nobody wrote down when it was planted. The Danish Dendrological Society surveyed Assistens in November 2019, put a GPS point on this tree, measured 1.4 metres around its stems and recorded it alive and healthy. That is the honest limit of what is known here: a girth, not an age. The range on this page is inferred from that measurement and from how recently the species arrived in Danish gardens, not read off any record.

It stands in section A of a cemetery Copenhagen treats as a park. People run, read and eat their lunch here, a few hundred metres from the graves of Hans Christian Andersen and Søren Kierkegaard.

best_time.label: May, when the bracts open and the Danish name for it, dove tree, makes sense

trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 5-7 minute walk; the station sits at the cemetery's northeastern corner, close to this tree

trees.name: The Weeping Beech of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section B, just right of the entrance from Kapelvej, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Every weeping beech is a graft, and on this one the join is in plain sight. About a metre up the trunk there is a visible union where a cutting of the pendulous form was fixed onto ordinary beech rootstock, and the surveyor who measured the tree in November 2019 noted that the grafted top is now putting on wood faster than the stock beneath it, so the trunk steps outward where the two meet. Look for that step before you look at the curtain.

The same survey recorded something less comfortable: a large wound at the base of the trunk. The tree was logged as alive, 3.29 metres round and 15 metres tall, but it is a healthy crown standing over an open injury, which is worth knowing rather than glossing over.

Weeping beech became a Danish cemetery fashion in the nineteenth century under the name sørgebøg, mourning beech, planted to hang over a grave the way a mourner leans over it. No planting date survives for this one. The 80 to 150 years on this page is worked back from the girth, not counted.

It stands in section B, just right of the Kapelvej entrance, which makes it the first serious tree most visitors to Assistens Kirkegård walk straight past.
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen) or the Kapelvej main entrance, roughly 5-10 minute walk

trees.name: The Great Maple of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section C, roughly 10m southwest of the section's centre, Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
The thickest tree at Assistens is also the least exotic species in it. At 4.19 metres round, this sycamore out-measures every tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these walls, including the rarities people actually come to see, and it does it as a common European maple that seeds itself into any gap it can find. Twenty-two and a half metres tall, one trunk to about two metres up and then a fork into two, alive and healthy at the November 2019 survey, rated regionally noteworthy.

Assistens was not built for strolling. It opened in 1757 outside the city ramparts as an overflow burial ground, taking the dead that Copenhagen's crowded parish churchyards could no longer hold, and the famous names arrived later. The city then grew out past it, Nørrebro packed in around it, and the place slowly turned into what it is now: a walled park with graves in it, where on a warm afternoon the living comfortably outnumber the mourners.

No planting date exists for this maple, and the 100 to 180 years given here is inferred from its girth rather than counted. What is certain is the measurement, taken with GPS in the field, and that nothing else registered in this cemetery is thicker. Section C, a little southwest of the section's centre.
trees.access: Free, open access; Assistens Kirkegård functions as both cemetery and public park, open 07:00-22:00 in summer and 07:00-19:00 in winter
trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 10 minute walk

trees.name: The Beech by the Boat Trip

location.address: Frederiksberg Have, beside the Bådfarten (rowing-boat rental/canal boat trip), Frederiksberg

trees.story:
This beech is registered under the name of a boat trip. Danish dendrologists filed it as Bøgen ved Bådfarten, the beech by the boat trip, which makes it the easiest tree on this list to find: walk to the jetty in Frederiksberg Have where the flat-bottomed boats set off around the canals, and the tree is the big one standing over you. Its trunk is 4.68 metres round and 1.49 metres across, measured in October 2016 and recorded alive.

The water it stands beside is the reason the garden looks the way it does. Frederiksberg Have began around 1700 as a Baroque layout of straight lines below the royal palace, then was redrawn between 1798 and 1804 into a romantic landscape of winding canals, islands and staged views, which is the fashion this beech grew up inside. The garden is protected under Danish conservation law and free to walk into.

Its age is not documented anywhere. The 120 to 220 years here comes from girth alone, and the garden's own heritage listing is careful on the point: the trees it names as three centuries old are the lindens on Mathildehøj, not this beech. Only one tree in our Copenhagen list carries a thicker trunk, and it is a short walk away in the same garden.

best_time.label: late October, when the copper leaves come down onto the canal below it

trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Allé metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-12 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance

trees.name: The Pedunculate Oak of Frederiksberg Have
trees.story:
This oak has no recorded birthday, but the garden gives it a ceiling. Frederiksberg Have was laid out as royal ground around 1700 and rebuilt between 1798 and 1804 into the romantic landscape park it still is, so whatever the tree's exact age, it cannot be older than the garden that had to exist before anyone planted in it. What was measured rather than guessed: 4.95 metres round, 28.8 metres tall, 1.58 metres through, surveyed by the Danish Dendrological Society in October 2016 and rated municipally noteworthy. That is the thickest trunk in our Copenhagen list.

The 130 to 250 years on this page is arithmetic on that girth against how fast a parkland oak puts on wood, not a date from any record, and it should be read as the wide guess it is. A pedunculate oak growing in the open with room on every side thickens faster than one shut into a wood, which is exactly the situation here, and one reason the upper end of that range is probably generous.

The garden around it is public, protected and busy: lawns, canals, the palace up on its hill, boats in summer. The oak has watched the whole thing turn from a royal retreat into the city's back garden.
trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Alle metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-15 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance

trees.name: The Honey Locust of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section E (near the middle of the section), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Someone has been keeping notes on this tree since 1941. That year a Danish gardening magazine ran a feature on beautiful trees and included a honey locust in section E of Assistens cemetery. In 1949 Jens Østergaard came to measure it for a nationwide survey of Gleditsia triacanthos in Danish gardens, published in the Dendrological Society's 1952 yearbook: twelve metres tall, standing on what the surveyor recorded as former rampart ground, clay loam, listed as site number six of only thirty-five in the whole country. In November 2019 the Society came back with a GPS and a tape. Sixteen metres, 1.18 metres round, alive and healthy.

Four metres of growth in seventy years is exactly what this species should manage, which is what makes the paper trail worth more than a plaque. The same tree, in the same spot, written up three times across eighty years by people with no reason to exaggerate.

The thorns are what to look for, and you will have to look up. Honey locust usually arms its trunk with branched spikes at chest height. This one carries only a few, sitting two and a half to three metres up, out of reach and easy to walk straight past.

Assistens opened in 1760 as a burial ground for the poor, on ground outside the city ramparts, and Hans Christian Andersen lies a few minutes' walk from here. The honey locust was rare enough in Denmark to be worth cataloguing nationally. It still is.

best_time.label: October, when the small leaflets turn clear yellow and come down almost at once

trees.name: The Pacifier Tree
trees.story:
Every November this hornbeam gets harvested. Since 2004 parents in Frederiksberg have brought toddlers here to tie up the pacifier they have agreed to give up, and once a year the whole crop comes down so the tree can start again. Danish dendrologists list it on their national register under the name everyone else uses: Suttetræet, the pacifier tree.

That register entry is unusual for what it leaves out. Every other tree recorded in Frederiksberg Have carries a height, a girth, often a planting year. This one carries none of them. Nobody has measured it and nobody has dated it, so read any age attached to this tree as a guess rather than a measurement. It is a mature garden hornbeam. That is the whole of what is known.

Which is rather the point. Carpinus betulus is the workhorse of formal European gardens, planted by the thousand for its density and its patience under the shears, and Frederiksberg Have has been royal ground since about 1700 and a romantic landscape park since its rebuilding between 1798 and 1804. The garden's history is documented down to the decade. The tree's is not. What it has instead is twenty-two years of small plastic objects and a steady supply of three-year-olds making a decision.

Come in autumn if you want to see it fully loaded. The November harvest clears it back to bare branches.
trees.access: Free, open access; Frederiksberg Have is a public park, protected (fredet) under Danish nature conservation law
trees.transport: Frederiksberg Alle metro station (M1/M2/M3), roughly 10-12 minute walk via Frederiksberg Runddel, the garden's main entrance

trees.name: The Sky-Reacher of Assistens

location.address: Assistens Kirkegård, Section F (north field, near Nørrebrogade/the station area), Nørrebro, Copenhagen

trees.story:
Skyrækker, the Danish name for this species, means sky-reacher. At 15.5 metres this one does not out-top the big beeches and maples around it, but at 4.01 metres round it is the largest exotic tree the Danish Dendrological Society registered inside these cemetery walls, and the only Ailanthus they found here at all.

It also comes with an open question. The surveyors who measured it in November 2019 logged its condition as levende, svag: alive, but weak. They noted severe bark scraping low on the western side of the trunk, the kind of injury that interrupts the traffic between roots and crown. Nothing found since updates that note, so what stands behind this entry is one careful observation now about seven years old. If you go and find it changed, tell us.

No source gives its age either. Somewhere between sixty and a hundred and twenty years is an inference from girth alone, not a record.

Ailanthus altissima reached Europe from China in the eighteenth century as a fashionable exotic and is now better known for pushing up through railway ballast and cracked concrete anywhere it can get a root down. This one was planted on purpose, in a cemetery that collected rarities, and the handkerchief tree and the ginkgo a few paths away come from the same appetite. Assistens works as a public park as much as a burial ground, and that collection is a large part of why.

trees.transport: Nørrebros Runddel metro station (M3 Cityringen), roughly 5-7 minute walk
